claim: The SAGA cohort represents 30% of the Icelandic nationwide female population aged 18-69 years.
source: All 18–69 year-old Icelandic speaking women residing in Iceland with an identifiable address or telephone number (n≈104,197), were invited to participate in the study from March 2018. Data collection continued until July 1st 2019, yielding a total of 30,403 participating women (30% of eligible women).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the sample size and percentage of eligible women who participated.

claim: The participants of the SAGA cohort represent the general Icelandic female population in terms of distribution of age, education level, geographical location, and monthly wages.
source: The participants of the SAGA cohort represent the general Icelandic female population in terms of distribution of age, education level, geographical location, and monthly wages (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript states representativeness and references a figure showing the distribution comparisons.

claim: The final study population consisted of 26,198 women after exclusions.
source: In addition, women who had more than 25% missing on perceived coping ability (n = 511), psychiatric resilience (n = 1040) and/or ACE-IQ (n = 93) were excluded, which resulted in a final study population of 26,198 women (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the final sample size after applying exclusion criteria.

claim: ACEs were measured with a modified version of the Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire (ACE-IQ) developed by the WHO.
source: ACEs were measured with a modified version of the Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire (ACE-IQ) developed by the WHO (WHO, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the measurement instrument and its source.

claim: The ACE-IQ instrument consists of 39 items assessing 13 types of adverse childhood experiences.
source: The instrument consists of 39 items assessing how often individuals were exposed to the following 13 ACEs during the first 18 years of their life: emotional neglect, physical neglect, emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, domestic violence, living with a household member who abuses drugs and/or alcohol, living with a household member who is mentally ill or suicidal, incarceration of a household member, parental death or separation/divorce, being bullied, witnessing community violence, and exposure to war/collective violence.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists the number of items and the 13 ACE types assessed.

claim: Perceived coping ability was assessed with the 10-item version of the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC-10).
source: Perceived coping ability was assessed with the 10-item version of the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC-10) (Campbell-Sills and Stein, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the measurement instrument used for perceived coping ability.

claim: The CD-RISC-10 has demonstrated good reliability and validity.
source: The scale, which measures individuals' perceptions of their ability to cope effectively with stress and adversity, such as the ability to adapt to change, achieving goals despite obstacles, and maintaining positivity in the face of stress, has demonstrated good reliability and validity (Campbell-Sills and Stein, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript states the psychometric properties of the scale with a citation.

claim: Psychiatric resilience was defined as absence of or low psychiatric morbidity among women exposed to lifetime trauma.
source: Consistent with previous literature (Choi et al., 2019; Nishimi et al., 2021; Stein et al., 2019) psychiatric resilience was defined as absence of or low psychiatric morbidity among women exposed to lifetime trauma, that is total sum of the inverse number of above-threshold symptom levels on PTSD, trauma-related sleep disturbances, binge drinking, depression, and anxiety.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines psychiatric resilience and cites previous literature supporting this definition.

claim: A clinical cut-off score of ≥33 on the PCL-5 was used to indicate probable PTSD.
source: A clinical cut-off score of ≥33 was used to indicate probable PTSD (Weathers et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the cut-off score with a citation.

claim: A clinical cut-off score of ≥4 on the PSQI-A was used to discriminate between participants with and without trauma-related sleep disturbances.
source: A clinical cut-off score of ≥4 was used to discriminate between participants with and without trauma-related sleep disturbances (Germain et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the cut-off score with a citation.

claim: Binge drinking was defined as having six or more units of alcohol on a single occasion at least once a month during the last year.
source: Binge drinking was defined as having six or more units of alcohol on a single occasion (one unit corresponds to a single measure of spirits) at least once a month during the last year (Bush et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines binge drinking with a citation.

claim: The standard cut-off score of ≥10 on the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 was used to indicate clinically relevant depression and anxiety.
source: The standard cut-off score of ≥10 was used, indicating clinically relevant depression and anxiety (Kroenke et al., 2001; Spitzer et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the cut-off scores with citations.

claim: 19.7% of participants reported no ACEs.
source: Overall, 19.7% of participants reported no ACEs and 20.4% reported five or more ACEs.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the percentage from descriptive statistics.

claim: 20.4% of participants reported five or more ACEs.
source: Overall, 19.7% of participants reported no ACEs and 20.4% reported five or more ACEs.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the percentage from descriptive statistics.

claim: Middle aged women had on average higher scores on the ACE-IQ than younger or older women.
source: Middle aged women had on average higher scores on the ACE-IQ than younger or older women.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this finding from descriptive analyses.

claim: Women with higher ACE scores were more often single or widowed, less educated, unemployed, had lower income and were more likely to report childhood deprivation and low perceived social support.
source: Women with higher ACE scores were more often single or widowed, less educated, unemployed, had lower income and were more likely to report childhood deprivation and low perceived social support (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript states these associations and references Table 1 showing the data.

claim: Perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience were moderately correlated (rs = 0.47).
source: The two resilience measures were moderately correlated (rs = 0.47).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the correlation coefficient.

claim: Perceived coping ability was moderately negatively correlated with each of the measures used to derive the psychiatric resilience phenotype (symptoms of depression, anxiety, PTSD, and trauma-related sleep disturbances).
source: Perceived coping ability was moderately negatively correlated with each of the measures used to derive the psychiatric resilience phenotype (i.e. symptoms of depression, anxiety, PTSD, and trauma-related sleep disturbances) but weakly correlated with binge drinking (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: The manuscript states the correlation patterns and references a table with the data.

claim: Perceived coping ability was weakly correlated with binge drinking.
source: Perceived coping ability was moderately negatively correlated with each of the measures used to derive the psychiatric resilience phenotype (i.e. symptoms of depression, anxiety, PTSD, and trauma-related sleep disturbances) but weakly correlated with binge drinking (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: The manuscript states the weak correlation and references a table.

claim: The 13 ACE subtypes were weakly to moderately correlated with each other (rs ranging from 0.06 to 0.46).
source: The 13 ACE subtypes were weakly to moderately correlated with each other (rs ranging from 0.06 to 0.46), with emotional abuse showing the strongest correlation with other ACEs (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the range of correlations and references a table.

claim: Emotional abuse showed the strongest correlation with other ACEs.
source: The 13 ACE subtypes were weakly to moderately correlated with each other (rs ranging from 0.06 to 0.46), with emotional abuse showing the strongest correlation with other ACEs (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and references a table.

claim: Every 1SD unit increase in ACE scores was associated with lower levels of coping ability (β = −0.14; 95% CI-0.15,–0.13) in the fully adjusted model.
source: every 1SD unit increase in ACE scores was associated with both lower levels of coping ability (β = −0.14; 95% CI-0.15,–0.13) and lower psychiatric resilience (β = −0.28; 95% CI-0.29,–0.27) in adulthood.
evidence: The manuscript reports the standardized regression coefficient with confidence interval from the analysis.

claim: Every 1SD unit increase in ACE scores was associated with lower psychiatric resilience (β = −0.28; 95% CI-0.29,–0.27) in the fully adjusted model.
source: every 1SD unit increase in ACE scores was associated with both lower levels of coping ability (β = −0.14; 95% CI-0.15,–0.13) and lower psychiatric resilience (β = −0.28; 95% CI-0.29,–0.27) in adulthood.
evidence: The manuscript reports the standardized regression coefficient with confidence interval from the analysis.

claim: Women with ≥5 ACEs had 36% lower prevalence of high coping ability (PR = 0.64, 95% CI 0.59,0.70) compared to women with 0 ACEs.
source: Compared to women with 0 ACEs, women with ≥5 ACEs had 36% lower prevalence of high coping ability (PR = 0.64, 95% CI 0.59,0.70) and 58% lower prevalence of high psychiatric resilience (PR = 0.42; 95% CI 0.39,0.45).
evidence: The manuscript reports the prevalence ratio with confidence interval from the analysis.

claim: Women with ≥5 ACEs had 58% lower prevalence of high psychiatric resilience (PR = 0.42; 95% CI 0.39,0.45) compared to women with 0 ACEs.
source: Compared to women with 0 ACEs, women with ≥5 ACEs had 36% lower prevalence of high coping ability (PR = 0.64, 95% CI 0.59,0.70) and 58% lower prevalence of high psychiatric resilience (PR = 0.42; 95% CI 0.39,0.45).
evidence: The manuscript reports the prevalence ratio with confidence interval from the analysis.

claim: Emotional neglect, bullying, sexual abuse and mental illness of household member were consistently associated with reduced adult resilience.
source: Specific ACEs including emotional neglect, bullying, sexual abuse and mental illness of household member were consistently associated with reduced adult resilience.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which specific ACEs showed consistent associations.

claim: The associations between ACEs and adult resilience were only slightly attenuated after controlling for adult socioeconomic factors and social support in adulthood.
source: We observed only slightly attenuated associations after controlling for adult socioeconomic factors and social support in adulthood.
evidence: The manuscript states the result of additional adjustment for potential mediators.

claim: Number of ACEs was inversely associated with adult resilience in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Number of ACEs was inversely associated with adult resilience in a dose-dependent manner
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the dose-response relationship observed in the data.

claim: Exposure to one or more ACEs (relative to 0 ACEs) was associated with lower perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Linear models revealed that exposure to one or more ACEs (relative to 0 ACEs) was associated with lower perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience in a dose-dependent manner (Table 3)
evidence: The manuscript states the finding from linear models and references the table with results.

claim: Associations between ACEs and perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience were observed across levels of social support but were slightly stronger among women with low social support.
source: Associations between ACEs and perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience were observed across levels of social support but were slightly stronger among women with low social support (Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from stratified analyses and references a table.

claim: The associations between ACEs and resilience remained evident when excluding parental separation/divorce from the ACE-IQ score.
source: Sensitivity analyses showed that the associations remained evident when excluding parental separation/divorce from the ACE-IQ score (Appendix 1—table 5)
evidence: The manuscript reports results from sensitivity analyses and references a table.

claim: The associations between ACEs and resilience remained evident when excluding women with top/bottom 10% happiness values.
source: Sensitivity analyses showed that the associations remained evident when excluding parental separation/divorce from the ACE-IQ score (Appendix 1—table 5), and when excluding women with top/bottom 10% happiness values (Appendix 1—table 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from sensitivity analyses and references a table.

claim: Every unit increase in the ACE-IQ scores was associated with lower prevalence of high perceived coping ability (PR = 0.93, 95% CI 0.92, 0.94).
source: Every unit increase in the ACE-IQ scores was associated with lower prevalence of high perceived coping ability (PR = 0.93, 95% CI 0.92, 0.94) and high psychiatric resilience (PR = 0.87, 95% CI 0.86, 0.87).
evidence: The manuscript reports the prevalence ratio with confidence interval from Poisson models.

claim: Every unit increase in the ACE-IQ scores was associated with lower prevalence of high psychiatric resilience (PR = 0.87, 95% CI 0.86, 0.87).
source: Every unit increase in the ACE-IQ scores was associated with lower prevalence of high perceived coping ability (PR = 0.93, 95% CI 0.92, 0.94) and high psychiatric resilience (PR = 0.87, 95% CI 0.86, 0.87).
evidence: The manuscript reports the prevalence ratio with confidence interval from Poisson models.

claim: All ACE subtypes were associated with lower levels of perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience.
source: All ACE subtypes were associated with lower levels of perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience (Appendix 1—figure 5)
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references a figure showing the results.

claim: After mutual adjustment for all ACE subtypes, emotional neglect, being bullied, sexual abuse, and growing up with a mentally ill household member had consistent associations with both resilience measures.
source: After mutual adjustment for all ACE subtypes, we found that emotional neglect, being bullied, sexual abuse, and growing up with a mentally ill household member had consistent associations with both resilience measures, both in linear models (Figure 1) and Poisson models (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from mutually adjusted models and references figures.

claim: Associations were suggested for emotional abuse, domestic- and community violence with psychiatric resilience in the full model.
source: Associations were also suggested for emotional abuse, domestic- and community violence with psychiatric resilience in the full model while associations for other ACEs were substantially attenuated (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from the full model and references figures.

claim: The results of the complete case analyses were similar to the results using multiple imputation in terms of both effect sizes and confidence intervals.
source: Overall, the results of the complete case analyses were similar to the results using multiple imputation (main analyses) in terms of both effect sizes and confidence intervals.
evidence: The manuscript compares results from different analytical approaches.

claim: ACEs have consistently been associated with elevated risk of multiple adverse health outcomes.
source: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) have consistently been associated with elevated risk of multiple adverse health outcomes, yet their contribution to coping ability and psychiatric resilience in adulthood is unclear.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The contribution of ACEs to coping ability and psychiatric resilience in adulthood is unclear.
source: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) have consistently been associated with elevated risk of multiple adverse health outcomes, yet their contribution to coping ability and psychiatric resilience in adulthood is unclear.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in the literature that motivates the study.

claim: Exposure to adverse childhood experiences is associated with elevated risk of a wide range of physical and mental health problems across the life course.
source: Exposure to adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), including child abuse, neglect and growing up in dysfunctional households, is associated with elevated risk of a wide range of physical and mental health problems across the life course (Anda et al., 2006; Bellis et al., 2015; Hughes et al., 2017; Petruccelli et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: Adult health outcomes most clearly associated with ACEs include problematic alcohol consumption and substance use, violence, and mental illness.
source: The results from a recent meta-analysis (Hughes et al., 2017) suggest that the adult health outcomes most clearly associated with ACEs include problematic alcohol consumption and substance use, violence, and mental illness.
evidence: The manuscript cites a meta-analysis supporting this claim.

claim: There is great variation in long-term outcomes of children exposed to ACEs.
source: However, there is great variation in long-term outcomes of children exposed to ACEs, and many children remain healthy despite excessive ACE exposure.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an observation from the literature.

claim: A substantial proportion of individuals exposed to ACEs do not develop mental illness in adulthood.
source: Importantly, it has been documented that a substantial proportion of individuals exposed to ACEs do not develop mental illness in adulthood (Green et al., 2010; Kessler et al., 2010), but instead exhibit resilience (Holmes et al., 2015; DuMont et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies documenting this phenomenon.

claim: Resilience is generally conceptualized as maintained mental health or positive adaptation despite trauma exposure.
source: Resilience is generally conceptualized as maintained mental health or positive adaptation despite trauma exposure (Luthar et al., 2000; Kalisch et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2019; Rutter, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple sources defining resilience.

claim: The complexity of the resilience concept has contributed to varying definitions and measurement approaches.
source: And although the scientific investigation of resilience can be traced back to the 1970s (Luthar et al., 2015; Masten et al., 2008; Garmezy, 1974; Garmezy, 1990; Werner, 1989; Rutter, 1990), the complexity of the concept has to date contributed to varying definitions and measurement approaches (Southwick et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature discussing the complexity of resilience measurement.

claim: Two common contemporary approaches to operationalize resilience among adults define it as perceived coping ability and as psychiatric resilience.
source: Two common contemporary approaches to operationalize the concept among adults, define resilience as perceived coping ability reflecting individuals' perceptions of their ability to cope effectively with stress and adversity (Campbell-Sills and Stein, 2007; Connor and Davidson, 2003), and as psychiatric resilience reflecting an empirically derived outcome, such as the absence of PTSD or other psychiatric disorders among individuals exposed to traumatic events (Nishimi et al., 2021; Sheerin et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing these two approaches.

claim: Psychiatric resilience is never directly measured as it consists of two separate components, trauma exposure and positive adaptation.
source: Indeed, it is important to note that psychiatric resilience is never directly measured as it consists of two separate components, trauma exposure and positive adaptation, and is therefore indirectly ascertained based on evidence of the two components (Luthar, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a source explaining the measurement of psychiatric resilience.

claim: The different resilience definitions (perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience) are not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary and may capture different underlying dimensions of resilience.
source: The different resilience definitions (i.e. perceived coping ability and psychiatric resilience) are not mutually exclusive, but rather complementary and may capture different underlying dimensions of resilience (Choi et al., 2019; Sheerin et al., 2018; Fisher and Law, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting this conceptualization.

claim: Only a handful of previous studies have addressed the association between ACEs and adult resilience.
source: Only a handful of previous studies have addressed the association between ACEs and adult resilience.
evidence: The manuscript characterizes the state of the literature.

claim: Childhood maltreatment has been negatively associated with psychiatric resilience in adulthood.
source: Childhood maltreatment, variously defined, has been negatively associated with psychiatric resilience (Mersky and Topitzes, 2010; Topitzes et al., 2013; McGloin and Widom, 2001; Williams et al., 2006) and perceived coping ability (Campbell-Sills et al., 2009; Nishimi et al., 2020) in adulthood.
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies showing this association.

claim: Childhood maltreatment has been negatively associated with perceived coping ability in adulthood.
source: Childhood maltreatment, variously defined, has been negatively associated with psychiatric resilience (Mersky and Topitzes, 2010; Topitzes et al., 2013; McGloin and Widom, 2001; Williams et al., 2006) and perceived coping ability (Campbell-Sills et al., 2009; Nishimi et al., 2020) in adulthood.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing this association.

claim: Most previous studies on ACEs and resilience have focused solely on childhood maltreatment or included only a small number of ACEs.
source: However, most studies have focused solely on childhood maltreatment or included only a small number of ACEs.
evidence: The manuscript characterizes limitations of previous research.

claim: Little is known about the association between cumulative ACE exposure and adult resilience.
source: Therefore, to date, little is known about the association between cumulative ACE exposure and adult resilience, and whether specific ACE types are to a varying extent associated with resilience.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: It is unclear whether specific ACE types are to a varying extent associated with resilience.
source: Therefore, to date, little is known about the association between cumulative ACE exposure and adult resilience, and whether specific ACE types are to a varying extent associated with resilience.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a research question.

claim: The study aimed to investigate the association between the cumulative number of a broad spectrum of ACEs and two distinct measures of adult resilience.
source: Leveraging a large nationwide study of Icelandic women, we aimed to investigate the association between the cumulative number of a broad spectrum of ACEs and two distinct measures of adult resilience, that is perceived coping ability and an outcome-based measure of low psychiatric morbidity.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the study aims.

claim: The study is the first to consider a wide range of ACEs in relation to adult resilience.
source: To our knowledge, the present study is the first to consider a wide range of ACEs in relation to adult resilience, and to address their association with two distinct resilience measures.
evidence: The manuscript claims novelty based on the scope of ACEs examined.

claim: The study is the first to address the association between ACEs and two distinct resilience measures.
source: To our knowledge, the present study is the first to consider a wide range of ACEs in relation to adult resilience, and to address their association with two distinct resilience measures.
evidence: The manuscript claims novelty based on examining two resilience measures.

claim: The study results are in line with previous studies examining the association between childhood maltreatment and adult resilience.
source: Overall, our results are in line with previous studies examining the association between childhood maltreatment and adult resilience (Mersky and Topitzes, 2010; Topitzes et al., 2013; McGloin and Widom, 2001; Williams et al., 2006; Campbell-Sills et al., 2009; Nishimi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript compares findings to previous literature.

claim: The existing evidence base on ACEs and resilience is limited by relatively small sample sizes.
source: However, the existing evidence base is limited by relatively small sample sizes, consideration of only few ACEs (McGloin and Widom, 2001; Williams et al., 2006; Campbell-Sills et al., 2009; Nishimi et al., 2020), and/or the use of composite measures of childhood adversity (Mersky and Topitzes, 2010; Topitzes et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript critiques previous literature with citations.

claim: The dose-response relationship between cumulative number of ACEs and lower adult resilience is consistent with a recent cross-sectional study by Nishimi et al., 2020.
source: Our results indicating a dose-response relationship between the cumulative number of ACEs and lower adult resilience is consistent with a recent cross-sectional study by Nishimi et al., 2020 who observed a similar pattern between four ACEs (emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, and witnessing domestic violence) and perceived coping ability, as measured with the CD-RISC.
evidence: The manuscript compares findings to a specific previous study.

claim: The study extended previous findings to psychiatric resilience as an outcome.
source: We have now extended these findings to psychiatric resilience as an outcome, and further demonstrated this pattern for a broad set of ACEs in a large nationwide study representing 30% of the Icelandic female population.
evidence: The manuscript describes how the current study extends previous work.

claim: Self-assessed coping ability and outcome-based psychiatric resilience were only moderately correlated with each other, indicating these may reflect different patterns of adaptive functioning following adversity.
source: In line with previous literature (Nishimi et al., 2021; Sheerin et al., 2018), we found that self-assessed coping ability and outcome-based psychiatric resilience were only moderately correlated with each other, indicating these may reflect different patterns of adaptive functioning following adversity.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the correlation finding with reference to previous literature.

claim: The associations between ACEs and adult resilience were independent of age, childhood deprivation and adult socio-demographic factors.
source: The associations between ACEs and adult resilience were independent of age, childhood deprivation and, importantly, other adult socio-demographic factors (i.e. educational level, civil status, employment level and income), suggesting that ACEs affect resilience over and above these potential mediating variables.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from adjusted models.

claim: ACEs affect resilience over and above potential mediating variables such as educational level, civil status, employment level and income.
source: The associations between ACEs and adult resilience were independent of age, childhood deprivation and, importantly, other adult socio-demographic factors (i.e. educational level, civil status, employment level and income), suggesting that ACEs affect resilience over and above these potential mediating variables.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the persistence of associations after adjustment.

claim: One possible mechanism through which ACEs could influence resilience is through functional outcomes in adulthood (e.g. social, financial and/or educational functioning).
source: Indeed, one possible mechanism through which ACEs could influence resilience, are functional outcomes in adulthood (e.g. social, financial and/or educational functioning).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a potential mechanism.

claim: ACEs are associated with greater risk of poor educational and financial outcomes, as well as poor social functioning.
source: Previous research has found that ACEs are associated with greater risk of poor educational and financial outcomes, as well as poor social functioning (Bellis et al., 2014; Copeland et al., 2018)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research supporting this claim.

claim: Adult factors such as education and employment level do not compensate for the deleterious impact of ACEs on adult resilience.
source: However, in the current study, effect sizes only diminished slightly when we additionally adjusted for adult socio-demographic factors, which indicates that adult characteristics such as education and employment level do not compensate for the deleterious impact of ACEs on adult resilience.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the minimal attenuation of effect sizes after adjustment.

claim: Adult resilience may largely be determined in childhood.
source: This suggests that adult resilience may largely be determined in childhood and that situational factors in adulthood (e.g. high social support) only marginally buffer the association between ACEs and adult resilience.
evidence: The manuscript infers this conclusion from the persistence of associations after adjustment.

claim: Situational factors in adulthood (e.g. high social support) only marginally buffer the association between ACEs and adult resilience.
source: This suggests that adult resilience may largely be determined in childhood and that situational factors in adulthood (e.g. high social support) only marginally buffer the association between ACEs and adult resilience.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the stratified analyses showing only slight differences by social support.

claim: The population-based design and large sample size of the SAGA cohort is a main strength of the study.
source: The main strengths of the study include the population-based design and large sample size of the SAGA cohort, which represents the Icelandic adult female population in terms of distribution of age, residence, education and income.
evidence: The manuscript identifies study strengths.

claim: The wealth of measures in the SAGA cohort baseline assessments made it possible to derive two types of resilience measures and examine a wide range of ACEs.
source: The wealth of measures in the SAGA cohort baseline assessments made it possible to derive two types of resilience measures and examine a wide range of ACEs.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a study strength.

claim: The study adjusted for childhood deprivation, an important confounder when examining ACEs and adult outcomes.
source: The wealth of relevant data also allowed us to adjust for childhood deprivation, an important confounder when examining ACEs and adult outcomes (Copeland et al., 2018; Arseneault et al., 2011; Bellis et al., 2017), which has not been taken into account in previous ACE-resilience studies.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a methodological strength with citations supporting the importance of this adjustment.

claim: Previous ACE-resilience studies have not taken childhood deprivation into account.
source: The wealth of relevant data also allowed us to adjust for childhood deprivation, an important confounder when examining ACEs and adult outcomes (Copeland et al., 2018; Arseneault et al., 2011; Bellis et al., 2017), which has not been taken into account in previous ACE-resilience studies.
evidence: The manuscript characterizes a limitation of previous research.

source: First, the cross-sectional nature of our data does not allow us to make any inferences about the directionality of the studied associations.

source: Second, we cannot rule out that the observed association between ACE growing up with a mentally ill household member and resilience, is due to a genetic predisposition for psychopathology rather than the experience itself.

source: Although we adjusted for an array of important confounding factors, we cannot exclude the possibility that unmeasured or residual confounding may contribute to our results.

source: In addition, ACEs were retrospectively reported and thus may be subject to recall bias.

source: However, previous studies have shown acceptable validity for retrospective assessments of ACEs (Reuben et al., 2016; Hardt and Rutter, 2004; Widom and Shepard, 1996; Widom and Morris, 1997), although they may be influenced by current mental health status or response style (Reuben et al., 2016).

source: However, previous studies have shown acceptable validity for retrospective assessments of ACEs (Reuben et al., 2016; Hardt and Rutter, 2004; Widom and Shepard, 1996; Widom and Morris, 1997), although they may be influenced by current mental health status or response style (Reuben et al., 2016).

source: Finally, our results are based on an exclusively female sample, therefore, future studies should explore whether there are qualitative differences in how ACEs relate to adult resilience among men as well as among sexual and gender minorities.

source: Finally, our results are based on an exclusively female sample, therefore, future studies should explore whether there are qualitative differences in how ACEs relate to adult resilience among men as well as among sexual and gender minorities.

source: In conclusion, in a large nationwide-representative female population, we observed a negative association between cumulative exposure of ACEs and two distinct measures of adult resilience.

source: Specific ACEs, including exposure to emotional neglect and bullying, sexual abuse, and growing up with a mentally ill household member were consistently associated with lower adult resilience.
